claims.claim: survival to metamorphosis is predicted to average about 5.3 % in freshwater species against 0.12 % in marine ones (Houde 1994, abstract)
claims.note: the abstract does say 'Predicted mean survivorship to metamorphosis of a cohort of freshwater fish larvae is 5.30%, while that of marine larvae is only 0.12%' — the paper's wording matches it and already says '(abstract)'; how the prediction was made (from which mortality and stage-duration values, at what temperature) needs the full text
as above: the abstract's 5.30 % is a model prediction for an average freshwater cohort, not a field measurement

redirected to a 'verify' puzzle page: not passed

notes: From the abstract (not usable as confirmation): after correcting for temperature, marine larvae have higher mortality rates, higher metabolic requirements and longer larval stages than freshwater larvae, with similar growth rates; expected survivorship of freshwater larvae is 44 times that of marine larvae; 'Starvation mortality is more probable for marine larvae', mainly because of their small size; episodic larval mortality may matter more to recruitment in freshwater fish, and juvenile-stage dynamics more than larval ones. These bear directly on §3.6.5's starvation paragraph. (The OUP abstract has a typo: marine larvae 'can be shown to experience mortality rates' — a word such as 'higher' is missing.)
